extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and general readers interested in aesthetic theory and evaluating art
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for judging whether a production is genuine art or a counterfeit — what art must do, what conditions must obtain in the artist, and what common methods produce mere imitations. Useful for artists evaluating their aims and critics assessing works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission (infection) of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of art lies in making that understood and felt which, in the form of an argument, might be incomprehensible; art must infect people with the emotion the artist has experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central test: does the work 'infect' others with the artist's feeling? If a work does not evoke the artist's feeling in recipients, it fails as art. Quoted examples of genuine transmis­sion include the Iliad, the Gospel parables, and folk-songs. If art fails to move people, the reasonable conclusion is that it is bad art or not art at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Great works of art are only great because they are accessible and comprehensible to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true work of art speaks a language understood across classes and cultures (e.g., Genesis, Gospel parables, folk-legends). Translation and cultural difference do not negate infection: a translated Joseph should touch a Chinese reader. Thus incomprehensibility to the masses usually indicates bad art, not a deficiency in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from specialised intellectual preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is differentiated from activity of the understanding (which demands preparation and sequence of knowledge) by the fact that it acts on people independently of their state of development and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic impact should not require prior technical study or stepwise intellectual training (unlike learning trigonometry from geometry). If understanding requires specialised preparation, the work is closer to a cognitive exercise than to universal art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of form and content (completeness, oneness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief characteristic of a work of art is completeness, oneness, the inseparable unity of form and contents expressing the feeling the artist has experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine artwork integrates feeling, content, and form so that the feeling cannot be separated from the form used. Works that lack this unity (for instance, those constructed mainly from borrowed material) simulate art but cannot produce true artistic infection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / sincerity of the artist
rubrics_metrics.description: A real artist transmits a feeling he has himself experienced; art must arise from the artist's inner impulse rather than being produced at will to meet demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art cannot be manufactured 'à froid' by mere technique or by following recipes; it must come from an experienced feeling and the artist's genuine desire and capacity to communicate it. Insincerity or atrophied aesthetic feeling leads to counterfeits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary artist conditions for true art
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce a real work of art it is necessary that the artist stand on the level of the highest life-conception of his time, experience feeling, have the desire and capacity to transmit it, and have talent for one of the forms of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All these conditions are seldom combined. 'Talent' here is the technical ability appropriate to the art (e.g., literary facility, power of visual memory, musical skill), but talent without the other conditions yields counterfeits. This is a checklist for whether a creator can produce genuine art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: Borrowing (the 'poetic' by imitation of past art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first counterfeit method is borrowing whole subjects or features from former works recognised as poetical, reshaping them to appear novel (so-called 'poetical subjects' and 'poetical people/objects').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing merely recalls prior artistic impressions and transmits someone else's feeling rather than the artist's own; it simulates art and may deceive audiences with perverted taste. Examples: using commonly recycled poetical objects (maidens, mountains, moonlight) to evoke a false poetic feeling; the authoress who rings the changes on poetic memories but has nothing of her own to say.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: Imitation / realism (excessive descriptive detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second counterfeit method is imitating real life by describing minutiae—the external appearance, gestures, clothes, environments—so that art becomes like photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-descriptive detail diverts the receiver's attention and hinders transmission of feeling; realism is no proof of artistic excellence and often indicates a counterfeit. In drama and literature, the habit of reporting disjointed real-life speech or excessive stage accessories similarly obstructs infection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: Striking / effectfulness (physiological effects and shocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third method imparts a semblance of art by producing physical or nervous effects—contrasts, the horrible, spectacular stage devices, pornographic or gruesome detail, loud orchestral crashes, crescendos, or other startling devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological reactions (tears from noise, excitement from spectacle) are not proof of transmitted feeling. Examples: stage deaths, darkness plus dismal music, or overuse of contrast; a single prolonged organ note may move the nerves but does not constitute music that transmits feeling. Confusing nervous stimulation with art is an important anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: Interestingness / puzzle/obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth counterfeit method is 'interestingness'—intricate plots, exotic detail, or constructed obscurities that compel the audience to puzzle, guess, or learn; the pleasure of discovery is mistaken for artistic infection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a work's aesthetic impact depends on supplying new information or on the mental effort of guessing, that effort distracts and hinders infection. Obscurity and the deliberate enigma in poetry (theory of obscurity) are criticised as substitutes for genuine artistic transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skill alone does not equal art
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of technical ability (the knack of rhyme, facility in description, drawing and modelling skill, musical dexterity and knowledge of counterpoint/orchestration) enables production but does not supply the essential quality of art—experienced feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical proficiency lets a person mass-produce convincing counterfeits by following recipes for different branches (poetry, novels, drama, painting, music). The text details how each art has its mechanical 'knacks' that, without feeling, yield imitation rather than true art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid market/professional incentive as primary motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerable remuneration and professionalisation of artists encourage the manufacture of counterfeits of art, because professional artists must continually invent subjects to please paying audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When art becomes a trade driven by demand of the upper classes, sincerity is weakened and formulaic counterfeits proliferate. This is a social/procedural criterion: be wary of works produced primarily to satisfy market tastes rather than to transmit sincere feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal criterion (religious perception) over external critical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal (true) art has a definite internal criterion—religious perception or the life‑conception shared by the people—whereas upper‑class art lacks this and relies on external criteria (critics, traditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on 'judgments of the finest-nurtured' or the authority of critics and tradition is misleading. Critics often lack susceptibility to infection and thus promulgate standards that perpetuate imitation and perversion of taste. The correct standard is internal transmission of feeling rooted in the common religious/life perception.
